<Callout title="Rolling out">
The updater service runs on Teire's server and is measured below. Fix runs move to it one ecosystem at a time, each once its upgrades pass on a real repository. Until an ecosystem moves, Teire's own transaction edits its manifest and lockfile, and the [verification](/docs/build/verification) is the same either way.
</Callout>

Changing a version in `package.json` is the easy part. Resolving the new lockfile, moving every declaration across workspaces, and knowing which other packages must move too is what package managers spend years getting right. Teire doesn't reimplement that. It runs **dependabot-core's updater** (MIT), through GitHub's `dependabot` CLI, and builds its own work on top: finding the lines that break, fixing them, and proving the fix.

## One job per upgrade

For each upgrade Teire decides on, it runs one updater job:

| Job | What it asks for |
|---|---|
| Version update | Exactly the target version Teire chose: only this dependency, nothing above the target, no extra cooldown (Teire already applied the repository's) |
| Security update | The lowest version that fixes the advisories that have a published fix |

Refresh and group-refresh jobs are built too. Until they are wired in, a base change re-runs the version or security job, which gives the same files.

A package declared in several lockfile roots runs as **one** job listing every root the same package manager covers (npm and Yarn roots together), so one pull request carries every root's change.

The job is bound to the commit Teire scanned, and the run returns the sha256 of the tarball it used.

## What comes back

The updater reports what it did as events. Teire reads those events, never the exit code:

- **A change**:
  - the dependency files, byte for byte, including binary lockfiles, deletions, symlinks and executable bits;
  - every package the updater moved alongside the upgrade, listed in the PR with its old and new version;
  - the version the dependency actually landed on. A version below the target means "resolvable only up to here", and the PR says why.
- **A named stop**, quoted in the PR or issue. Examples: no set of versions satisfies every requirement; every newer version is ignored by the repository's configuration; no version that fixes the advisory has been published.
- **Nothing to change**: for a version update whose every newer version the repository ignores, the updater changes nothing, as Dependabot does. The run ends saying so.

## When the updater says no

There is no silent fallback. For an ecosystem that has moved to the updater:

| What came back | What Teire does |
|---|---|
| A change at the target | Applies it, then runs the [verification](/docs/build/verification) |
| A change below the target | Makes that version the target, compares its API again, and the PR opens with **Why X** quoting the reason |
| A security fix above the lowest published one | The lowest published fix doesn't resolve in this repository, so the updater's lowest fix becomes the target, as Dependabot's own security update would; the PR says why |
| A named stop | Opens one issue for the package, quoting the updater's words. The next pull request for that package closes it |
| Nothing to change | Ends the run with the reason |
| The updater is unreachable | Waits 15 minutes and tries again, up to three times, then stops with an issue |

Every file path is checked before it is used. A path that would leave the repository, or touch `.git`, is refused.

## Your dependabot.yml counts

If the repository has `.github/dependabot.yml`, the updater's jobs follow it:

- **Applied:** ignores (names, version ranges, update types), groups, the versioning strategy, `vendor`, `exclude-paths`, the commit message prefix, and `insecure-external-code-execution`.
- **Conflicts:** where `teire.yml` sets the same thing (commit prefix, target branch, PR limit), `teire.yml` wins, and the run's timeline says which file decided.
- **Not applied:** reviewers, assignees, milestones, labels, schedules and multi-ecosystem groups. Teire opens its own pull requests on its own schedule, so these don't reach the updater's job.

## Where it runs

The updater runs on Teire's own server, in a separate Docker daemon whose containers run under **gVisor**. gVisor is a kernel in user space: container system calls never reach the host's kernel directly.

| Boundary | Rule |
|---|---|
| Network | The updater sits on a network with no route out. Only Dependabot's proxy reaches the internet, and the host firewall stops it reaching Teire's apps, its database, cloud metadata and every host port except the job's own event API. Jobs run one at a time, so no job can reach another's |
| Credentials | A token that can only read this one repository, valid for an hour. The proxy holds it; the updater never does |
| Images | Dependabot's updater and proxy images, pinned by digest. The CLI checks their build attestations before use |
| Code execution | Off only when the job carries private-registry credentials and the repository hasn't allowed it, as Dependabot does |
| Resources | One job at a time; capped CPU and memory; a 20-minute limit, then everything the job started is removed |

The full threat model, and the probe that proves each point, is [in the repository](https://github.com/teire-dev/teire/blob/main/apps/resolver/THREAT-MODEL.md).

## What Teire still does itself

Some upgrades Dependabot doesn't do, so Teire keeps its own changes for them:

- Go majors, which move to a new module path (`/v5`);
- Cargo crates renamed in `Cargo.toml`; features a new version removed are dropped from the updater's input first, so it can reach that version (rand 0.10 removed `small_rng`);
- Gradle lockfiles: the updater rewrites every entry, so Teire keeps its build-file change and re-locks only the upgraded coordinate;
- npm aliases (`npm:`);
- pnpm lockfiles older than version 6 (pnpm 7), which the updater's pnpm reader fails on although pnpm reads them;
- Bun's binary `bun.lockb`, since the updater reads only the text `bun.lock` (Bun 1.1.39 and later);
- `pylock.toml`;
- a vulnerable transitive package the updater can't move within its parents' ranges: Teire pins the fix with npm `overrides`, pnpm `overrides`, or Yarn and Bun `resolutions`, and reads the new lockfile back. The same rung for the other ecosystems is planned; until then the run stops and says so.

Planned and not built yet: the runtime or build-tool bump a new major needs (Java 17 for Spring Boot 4, for example).

Then, for every upgrade, the [verification](/docs/build/verification) runs your own install, typecheck and tests before and after.
